opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that robotics today looks a lot like machine learning did maybe ten years ago. It's a field with brilliant people, but it's siloed. Every lab has its own hardware, its own data formats, its own training code, and it's really hard for someone outside those labs to just pick things up and start building. The barrier to entry is enormous: you need expensive hardware, you need deep expertise in control and perception, and you mostly need to reinvent the wheel each time.

What we saw with open-source AI, with Transformers and the Hub, is that when you lower that barrier and give people shared tools, shared models, and shared datasets, you suddenly get this explosion of creativity. Millions of developers who aren't PhDs in NLP started building with language models. Our vision is to do the same thing for robotics.

That's a few layers. First, software: a library like LeRobot where you can train a policy, share it, and load someone else's with a few lines of code, with standardized dataset formats so a recording from one robot is useful to someone else. Second, data: robotics is starved for data compared to language or vision, and the only way I see us getting to the scale we need is if a large community contributes, many people recording demonstrations on many different robots in many different environments. That's very open-source in spirit. Third, and this is the part people sometimes underestimate, hardware. If a robot arm costs tens of thousands of dollars, you'll never have a broad community. So we've been pushing on really low-cost, open-source designs, things you can 3D print and assemble for a couple hundred dollars, so a student or hobbyist can have a real robot on their desk.

When you combine those, cheap accessible hardware, shared datasets, and easy-to-use pretrained models, robotics stops being something that happens only in a handful of well-funded labs and becomes something anyone can tinker with. And I think that's where a lot of the most interesting progress will come from, just like it did for AI more broadly. The community will find use cases and ideas that none of us would have predicted.

r001.rationale: The response compares robotics to earlier machine learning and says millions of developers began building with language models, then states the vision is to do the same for robotics.

r002.rationale: It says shared tools, models, and datasets can lower barriers for developers, and describes software such as LeRobot that lets people train, share, and load robotics policies.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is really through the lens of what happened in NLP. When we started Hugging Face, working with language models was something a few hundred people in the world could really do. You needed to be inside a big lab, you needed the compute, you needed to know how to read the papers. And what changed everything was not a single breakthrough model, it was lowering the barrier. Transformers, the library, let you load a state-of-the-art model in three lines of code, and suddenly you had hundreds of thousands of people building on top of it, finding use cases nobody at the labs would have imagined.

Robotics today feels a lot like NLP did in 2017 or 2018. It's an incredibly exciting field, the foundation-model wave is clearly coming, but it's still mostly closed. The hardware is expensive, the software stacks are fragmented, every lab has its own setup, and the datasets, when they exist, are locked inside companies. So a student in Lagos or a developer in Lyon basically cannot participate, even if they have great ideas.

So the vision is to do for robotics what open source did for language. That means three things. First, affordable hardware. If a robot arm costs a hundred thousand dollars, you'll never have a community. If it costs a few hundred dollars and you can print parts of it, you get a hobbyist movement, and hobbyist movements are where a lot of real innovation starts. Second, a shared software layer, so that a policy you train on one setup can be shared, downloaded, fine-tuned by someone else, the way people share model checkpoints today. And third, open datasets. In robotics, data is the real bottleneck. We don't have the internet to scrape. So we need to pool it, and you only get that if thousands of people are recording their own demonstrations and contributing them back.

What I find most exciting is the feedback loop. Once the barrier is low enough, people stop asking permission. A teenager will teach a robot to fold laundry in their bedroom, and that becomes a dataset, and that becomes a demo that inspires ten other people. We've seen this movie before, and it ends with the open ecosystem moving faster than anyone expected. I think physical AI will be the same, and honestly, I think it should be, because robots in our homes is not a technology you want controlled by three companies.

r001.rationale: The candidate compares robotics to NLP’s shift toward broader participation, but does not draw the specific analogy between software developers becoming AI-aware and potentially becoming roboticists.

r002.rationale: It proposes affordable hardware, shared software, and open datasets to lower barriers, enabling developers and hobbyists to participate in building and training robots.

astra-6.text:
My vision is to make robotics much more like an open developer ecosystem, where you don’t need to be in a specialized lab to contribute. You should be able to get an affordable robot, download a model, try something, and share what you’ve learned.

That requires opening up the whole stack: the hardware designs, the software, the datasets, and the models. And the starting experience has to be simple. If you spend weeks configuring a robot before you can make it do anything, you lose a lot of people who could bring great ideas.

The exciting part is that people can contribute in different ways. Some will build better hardware, others will collect demonstrations, train models, or create applications. If those contributions can build on one another, robotics becomes something a much broader community can advance together.

r001.rationale: The response advocates a broader robotics developer ecosystem but does not compare software developers becoming AI-aware with their potentially becoming roboticists.

r002.rationale: It proposes affordable robots, downloadable models, an open stack, and a simple starting experience so a broader developer community can contribute to robotics.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d love to make robotics something that any developer can get started with. Today, there’s still a lot you have to figure out before you can even begin experimenting: the hardware, the software, collecting data, training a model. We need to make that first step much easier.

And I think open source is really important here. If we can share affordable robot designs, datasets, models, and tools, people can build on each other’s work. You shouldn’t need to build an entire robotics company just to try an idea.

The exciting moment is when people start doing things that we didn’t anticipate—building a robot for their own needs, sharing what worked, and helping someone else improve it. That’s how you move from a small group of specialists to a community of developers who can actually push the field forward.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making robotics accessible to developers, but it does not compare that shift to software developers broadly becoming AI-aware.

r002.rationale: It says affordable robot designs, datasets, models, and tools could make robotics easier for any developer to start exploring and building.
